name: Omar Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Omar. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to companies, unions, parties or government, and what you say is confidential. Could you tell me what a normal working day looks like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the corrugator at Norland Packaging. That's the big machine that makes cardboard, the wavy middle and the flat sheets glued together. It's about a hundred metres long, steam, glue, rolls of paper the size of a car. I lead a crew of five on the early shift, six to two. Most of the day I'm watching the glue and the moisture, because if the paper's too wet or too dry the board warps and the box plant downstream screams at me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's my machine. I know it the way you know an old car, every noise. When we break a speed record, the plant manager buys pastries for the crew, and I've had more of those than anyone. What wears me out is the heat in summer and the money. Best guy on the corrugator and I make less than the drivers who take the boxes away. Sofia, my girlfriend, works at the pharmacy, and between us we're fine until something breaks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. Never tried. Sofia uses one to write emails to her landlord, I mean our landlord. I just don't see the point for what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Yeah, I can see that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go. It was all over the news and then nothing much happened. That's what happens with most things. At work we'd talk about football again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad, but I wasn't very worried in the first place. The corrugator's not the kind of machine a computer just takes over. Too much steam and glue and guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep running my machine, keep my head down. Maybe try again for the shift allowance, because the early shift should pay more. I'd try to save a bit, but I say that every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you say you'll save every year. What usually happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something happens. Last year the car's clutch went, eight hundred. The year before, Sofia's mum needed help with her rent. It's never a big thing, it's just always a thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned guessing. What do you mean by that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the weather. If it rains for three days, the paper rolls soak up moisture in the warehouse, and you've got to change the steam and the glue by feel. The computer gives you numbers, but the numbers lie in the rain. I've got twelve years of rain in my head. Well, six on the corrugator.

S0.say: There you go, it was all over the news and nothing much happened. That's what happens with most things.
S0.think: I'd be glad, but I wasn't very worried anyway. The corrugator isn't a machine a computer simply takes over, with all its steam, glue and guessing.
S0.do: Keeps running the corrugator exactly as before and asks again for a better early shift allowance. Means to save a little but expects some bill to take it, as it does every year.
S0.quote: The computer gives you numbers, but the numbers lie in the rain.
S0.fieldNote: Omar's confidence rests on a craft he can describe precisely, reading paper moisture by feel. He doesn't blame anyone for low pay, he just notes it. His savings vanish into small emergencies, like the clutch and helping Sofia's mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. Many jobs. I'd want to know which ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see what actually changes before everyone panics. Companies will try things, some will work, some won't. I'm not going to be the guy shouting about robots in the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? I'd worry a bit. The guys at the end of the line, stacking and strapping the bundles, that's simple work for a robot arm. If they lose that, the crew gets smaller and maybe they don't need a lead. But my part, the moisture and the glue, I still think that's a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and watch. If they started talking about a new system for the corrugator, I'd want to be the person they ask about it, not the person they replace. But I'm not going to rush out and do a course on something that might not happen to me. Maybe I'd try harder with the savings, put a hundred aside after payday before I can spend it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. Like noticing a new noise from the machine and hoping it goes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want them to ask you about a new system. Have they ever asked you before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once. When they changed the glue kitchen, they asked me what I thought and then did it differently anyway. It worked out, mostly. So, half yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hope it goes away. Do you think it would?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Not really. But I've been wrong about new noises before, sometimes they do go away. I'll know more when I see what the box plant in the next town does. They always try things first.

S1.say: Let's see what actually changes before everyone panics. Companies will try things, some will work and some won't.
S1.think: The stacking and strapping at the end of the line is simple work for a robot arm, so the crew might shrink and need no lead. I still think the moisture and glue work stays with a person.
S1.do: Carries on and watches what the other box plant does first, hoping to be consulted on any new system. Refuses to take a course for something that might not affect him but tries to set aside 100 straight after payday.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, like a new noise from the machine he hopes will go away.
S1.quote: Like noticing a new noise from the machine and hoping it goes away.
S1.fieldNote: Omar's resistance shows as watchful patience rather than anger. He sees the risk clearly at the end of the line but believes his own part is safe. He admitted the noise probably won't go away, then fell back on waiting to see what the other plant does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. With the robots too. Okay. That's not a small thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know, nobody knows, let's not make it worse by panicking. That's what I'd say to the crew, anyway. Somebody's got to stay calm, and I'm the lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record? If a machine can read the board and change the glue, and a robot can do the splices, then I'm out. And there's nothing else here. The box plant in the next town would go the same way at the same time. I'd be thirty, no savings, a skill nobody needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything. The car, maybe, because it's paid off and I could sell it for a couple of thousand. Sofia and I would talk about moving in with my parents for a while to save rent. I'd start asking around for anything, delivery, building sites, anything that's still a person. I don't know what I'd be qualified for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. I wouldn't sleep. I'd lie there listening to Sofia breathe and doing the numbers in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would moving in with your parents go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would love it. My dad would make a speech about how he worked at the same foundry for thirty years, and then he'd shut up and help. Sofia would hate it. Their flat has one bathroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You told the crew to stay calm, but you'd be lying awake. Which one is the real you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. That's what a lead does. You keep it together on the floor and you fall apart at home. I've done it before, when we had the fire in the glue kitchen.

S2.say: Nobody knows, so let's not make it worse by panicking. Somebody's got to stay calm, and I'm the lead.
S2.think: If a machine can read the board and a robot can do the splices, I'm out. There's nothing else nearby, and I'd be thirty with no savings and a skill nobody needs.
S2.do: Cuts everything, possibly selling the paid-off car for a couple of thousand, and talks with Sofia about moving in with his parents to save rent. Starts asking around for any work that still needs a person, such as delivery or building sites.
S2.feel: Bad and sleepless, lying awake doing the numbers.
S2.quote: You keep it together on the floor and you fall apart at home.
S2.fieldNote: Omar separates his public role as calm lead from private fear, and he named that split himself. Fast AGI breaks his belief that the corrugator needs a person's feel. His fallback is family, his parents' one-bathroom flat, rather than any plan to learn something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. So I'd see the robots coming down the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, let's use it sensibly. Not panic, not pretend it's not coming. I'd probably say that to the crew in those words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough time for me to keep doing my job for most of it. That's the honest truth of how I'd think. I'd run the corrugator until they told me to stop, and I'd try to save as much as I could in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a proper savings plan, maybe two hundred a month, if Sofia and I cut the takeaways and I stop buying fishing gear. I'd keep running the machine. Maybe, around year three, I'd look at what's still hiring. I know I should do more than that. I'm just not someone who jumps early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not like the two-year one. More like a deadline at school you keep putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you know you should do more. What's stopping you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what to do. If someone told me, learn this and you're safe, I'd probably do it. But nobody can tell me that. So it's easier to keep doing what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sofia say about the fishing gear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd laugh. She's been telling me to stop buying lures for two years. I've got a box with forty of them. I'd sell some of them online, actually, that's real money.

S3.say: We've got time, so let's use it sensibly. That means not panicking and not pretending it's not coming, and I'd tell the crew that in those words.
S3.think: Five years means I'd keep doing my job for most of it, honestly. I'd run the corrugator until told to stop and save as much as I could meanwhile.
S3.do: Sets a savings plan of about 200 a month by cutting takeaways and fishing gear, and sells some of his 40 lures online. Keeps running the machine and plans to look at what's still hiring around year three.
S3.feel: Anxious, like a school deadline he keeps putting off.
S3.quote: If someone told me, learn this and you're safe, I'd probably do it. But nobody can tell me that.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Omar's plan is to save and keep working, and he admits he should do more. What holds him back is not knowing what to do, not laziness. The box of forty fishing lures gave a concrete, slightly comic picture of where his spare money goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's far enough away to feel like someone else's problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, a lot can happen. Governments will have to sort something out by then. I wouldn't make a big deal of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is about how long I'd want to stay on the corrugator anyway. My back won't love that heat at forty. So maybe it's fine, maybe the timing lines up. I'd still be worried about what comes after, but it's far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd keep going. I'd save, but the way I do now, badly. Maybe in a few years, once it's clear what's left for people, I'd think about learning a trade. My cousin does electrical work. But not now. Now I'd just keep running my machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, in the back of my head. Mostly I'd forget about it, then remember when the news is on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said with two years you'd lie awake, but with ten it feels like someone else's problem. Is that fair to future you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. Future me will be annoyed with me. But I've never been good at planning ten years out. I didn't plan the corrugator, I just got moved onto it when the old lead retired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be watching for, to know it's time to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When they stop replacing the guys who leave. That's always the sign at Norland. When someone retires and nobody new comes, you know they're planning something.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time and a lot can happen. Governments will have to sort something out by then.
S4.think: Ten years is about how long I'd want to stay on the corrugator anyway, because my back won't love the heat at forty. I'd still worry about what comes after, but it's far away.
S4.do: Keeps running the corrugator and saves in the same patchy way he does now. Plans to think about learning a trade, perhaps electrical work like his cousin, once it's clear what's left for people.
S4.feel: A background unease he mostly forgets until the news comes on.
S4.quote: Future me will be annoyed with me.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade Omar's resistance returns to plain waiting. He's honest that he doesn't plan far ahead and that this isn't fair to his future self. His early warning sign is staff not being replaced, which is how he reads change at Norland.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. I'd have no money and no idea what to do next, and there's nowhere else around here to go. What would help is someone actually telling me, here's a job that will still exist, and paying me while I learn it. I'd do it if I knew it was real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how many of us there are. Not the clever ones who'll be fine. Guys like me, good at one machine, not much else. I think there's a lot of us, and nobody's asking us.

headlineQuote: Not the clever ones who'll be fine. Guys like me, good at one machine, not much else.
portrait: Omar is a 27-year-old corrugator lead at a cardboard plant who reads paper moisture by feel and earns less than the drivers who take the boxes away. He lives with his girlfriend Sofia, a pharmacy worker, and his small savings keep vanishing into car repairs and family help. He doesn't blame anyone and prefers to wait and see, keeping calm in front of his crew even when he's frightened. Fast AGI leaves him sleepless and reaching for his parents' flat, while slower versions let him keep running his machine and put off deciding. He says he'd retrain if someone could show him a job that would really last.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd have no money, no idea what to do next and no other plants nearby.
whatWouldHelp: Someone telling him which job will still exist and paying him while he learns it.
